title: I'm not tempted to call an early election, Andy Burnham says
description: He was later asked by BBC East Midlands political editor Peter Saull if there would be a general election next May, alongside council elections in the
body: He was later asked by BBC East Midlands political editor Peter Saull if there would be a general election next May, alongside council elections in the area.The PM replied "no" before adding: "Not having a general election."Burnham also said he wanted to use the conference to say more about "the direction I want to take the country in", adding: "The focus is on that, helping people with the cost of living, helping businesses with the cost of running a business."These have got to be the priorities right now, rather than throwing the country into a backward-looking process where we're arguing again amongst ourselves."Burnham said he wanted to ensure people were "feeling a bit of hope in their lives again", adding: "That's what I'm trying to do, and I hope to take it further in the coming period, rather than putting people back into an election cycle."The prime minister was also asked about the number of migrants crossing the English Channel in small boats.It comes after 781 people were recorded arriving in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest total for a single day so far this year.Burnham said his goal was that he did not want to see any crossings "at all".He declined to put a timescale on this ambition, but said his government would "not stop" working until crossings went "right down".He argued that Brexit had hampered the UK's ability to stop the arrivals, saying it had led to a "loss of collaboration with neighbours".Elsewhere in the series of interviews, he said:He would not do any "special interviews" with the Sun - he told the BBC in 2015 that he had not forgiven the newspaper for its coverage of the 1989 Hillsborough disasterTourists would not "begrudge paying a few extra pounds" as a result of his proposal to allow regional mayors in England to charge new tax on visitors' overnight staysThe government would "do what we can within the resources that we've got to support people" in the Budget next month

schema.headline: I'm not tempted to call an early election, Andy Burnham says

title: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare
description: A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance.Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His c
body: A set of bumper local elections has thrown Germany, and its government, off balance.Chancellor Friedrich Merz may now be a man on borrowed time. His coalition government is in crisis.But this breakdown of business as usual in Germany has been brewing for years.It's a nation wrestling with new, uncomfortable and unresolved realities.Think of certain stereotypes about Germany, and think again.A country dominated by boring, consensus-driven politics? Not any more.A confident, powerhouse economy at the cutting edge of car-making? Yesterday's story.A nation that can be used as a byword for impressive efficiency? The trains don't even run on time.Many Germans I've spoken to feel their nation has drifted away from the things that once anchored their identity.And the question of what next is, as yet, unanswered.That uncertainty is currently embodied by a beleaguered chancellor weakened by bruising regional election results.In the last fortnight, Friedrich Merz's party was beaten to first place in Berlin, pummelled in the polls in Saxony-Anhalt and pushed out of parliament altogether in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.A lifeline for Merz is that no-one, within his own centre-right CDU party, is yet willing to challenge the chancellor openly despite persistent rumours of a Kanzlertausch (chancellor swap).But he is on thin ice, with record low approval ratings among voters who often describe him as arrogant and out of touch.It is a problem that in government circles is sometimes more politely referred to as a "communication" issue.Those who back the Chancellor say it is time to double down on much-needed reforms, alongside its centre-left SPD coalition partner, and find a better way of talking to people.Swapping chancellors is not the answer as anyone would face the "same challenges", argues Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy spokesperson in parliament for Merz's CDU and its sister party, the CSU.Hardt pointed out that the CDU/CSU fared far better in other regional elections earlier this year, when we spoke minutes after Merz addressed party lawmakers at a closed-door meeting in the Bundestag."I think Friedrich Merz knows about his deficits," says Hardt. "He will work on him and we will work on us as (a) party. And hopefully we will convince the people in the next months that we are on the right way."Merz came to power in 2025, promising to get tough on immigration and boost Germany's ailing economy.He appeared to offer a dynamism that might act as an antidote to the former dull, unhappy drumbeat of centre-left leader Olaf Scholz's bickering three-way coalition.And Merz's allies would claim he has had some success.This week, leading economic institutes raised the country's growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 above 1% while illegal entries into Germany – and Europe – are down year on year.But that will not eliminate public anxieties, on either issue.Households and businesses continue to endure high energy costs while fears persist that China is cannibalising German industry, including its iconic car sector.It is a brutal reversal of Germany's old recipe for success: cheap Russian gas that powered a booming export-driven economy.And when it comes to immigration, the focus is now less on new arrivals and more on concerns about public safety, welfare costs and integration.While there are local exceptions, voters appear to be losing faith in Germany's two principal governing parties (CDU and SPD).Enter the rising force in German politics, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD): a party that alarms security officials with its Russia-friendly stance and contains regional branches that are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence.Smears and misrepresentations, argues the AfD, as it claimed its third victory ever in a state election last Sunday in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-West Pomerania.Its co-leader, Alice Weidel, told me this week that Friedrich Merz's days were numbered.

schema.headline: As Merz scrambles for support, Germany's identity crisis is laid bare

title: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
description: South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikan
body: South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself."Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.His response to the US president's claim is blunt. The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property."Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa. "While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms". "There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners."I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy"  to speak about the subject.The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner". "But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of  further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked. He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement."South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington."It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

schema.headline: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC

title: Two sentenced for 2022 murder of Argentine former rugby player
description: Two men with links to the far-right have been jailed over the fatal shooting of a former Argentine international rugby player in the streets of Paris
body: Two men with links to the far-right have been jailed over the fatal shooting of a former Argentine international rugby player in the streets of Paris four years ago.Federico Martin Aramburu, who played more than twenty matches for Argentina, was killed in a drive-by shooting in 2022 after an early-morning fight broke out in a bar near Boulevard Saint-Germain.Loik Le Priol, 32, a former soldier who fired the fatal shots, was sentenced to 26 years in jail. Romain Bouvier, 35, who opened fire initially, was sentenced to 19 years in jail.In a Paris court on Friday, Le Priol asked Aramburu's family for forgiveness as the trial concluded. "I'm Christian like you, the pope is here today" he said, referring to Pope Leo XIV's visit to France."I don't know if it's a sign... [I] hope one day you can find the strength to forgive me," Le Priol continued.Former rugby star Aramburu was 42 when he was killed. He played for Argentina 22 times, including at the 2007 World Cup in France where he scored a try against the hosts to help his country finish third. The player also had spells at French clubs Perpignan, Biarritz and Dax before joining Glasgow Warriors in 2010.CCTV footage reviewed during the investigation showed Aramburu and his former rugby teammate, Shaun Hegarty, sitting at a bar opposite the former soldier, Le Priol, and his friend Bouvier on 19 March 2022. Le Priol and Bouvier were both linked to a far-right extremist group at the time, which has since dissolved.  An altercation broke out between the two groups of men, the CCTV footage showed. As the two former Rugby players walked off towards their hotel, Le Priol and Bouvier drove around to find them and opened fire. Aramburu died at the scene, Reuters reported. Le Priol was subsequently arrested in Hungary while attempting to cross the border ⁠into ​Ukraine. He told Hungarian police at the time he was going to Ukraine to fight.The defence cited post-traumatic stress disorder in Le Priol's case and childhood trauma in Bouvier's case.But in court, Le Priol was described as "animated by the will to kill". "The narcissistic, intrusive and uncontrollable rage of Loik Le Priol ultimately led to the gratuitous killing of Mr. Aramburu," the presiding judge said.Meanwhile, Aramburu's widow Maria asked for a verdict that would allow her and  Aramburu's three children "to build their lives as adults".

schema.headline: Two sentenced for 2022 murder of Argentine former rugby player

title: Sir David Beckham nets £38.5m after World Cup ad deals
description: Sir David Beckham has netted a £38.5m payout from his sports, fashion, and media business after the 2026 Men's Football World Cup helped it bring in r
body: Sir David Beckham has netted a £38.5m payout from his sports, fashion, and media business after the 2026 Men's Football World Cup helped it bring in record profits.The former England star's DRJB Holdings, which includes the Beckham brand, reported an almost £50m profit in 2025, a 46% jump compared to a year earlier. Sales rose from £72.2m to £84m.The rise was driven by a slew of advertising partnerships struck in the runup to the tournament, including with Bank of America, McDonald's, Verizon, and PepsiCo Lay's.Sir David, Britain's first billionaire sportsman, was commonly seen in adverts during the summer's World Cup.In the US, it was difficult for fans to watch a game without coming across Beckham in adverts for Stella Artois, Home Depot and Lay's crisps - known as Walkers in the UK.Sir David also launched menswear collections for Hugo Boss last year, as well as a pair of Adidas Predator football boots and an eyewear range with Italian glasses maker Safilo.Revenues at DRJB, of which Beckham owns almost half, were boosted by growth in Beckham's health supplements business too.DRJB paid its shareholders £38.9m, followed by a special £46.6m payment after the end of the financial year.Sir David's share of those dividends would have been around £38.5m due to how much of the company he owns.The remainder of DRJB is owned by New York-based Authentic Brands Group, which also owns Reebok, as well as the rights to other celebrity brands such as comedian and actor Kevin Hart.Authentic's entertainment chief executive Corey Salter said the performance showed Sir David's name is "one of the most powerful global brands in sport, lifestyle, entertainment and much more"."It's been an outstanding year, from new partnerships to important philanthropic campaigns and overall brand growth," he said.Sir David previously drew criticism for associating himself with a country where same-sex relationships are illegal by acting as an ambassador for the 2022 Men's Football World Cup in Qatar."It was an important competition and one I was proud to be part of," he said at the time, adding that he had engaged with the LGBTQ community during the tournament.

schema.headline: Sir David Beckham nets £38.5m after World Cup ad deals

title: Trump's plans for massive arch move ahead
description: Earlier this week Trump announced that the proposed "Triumphal Arch" would double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability
body: Earlier this week Trump announced that the proposed "Triumphal Arch" would double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones from the roof and plaza.In a letter to the Pentagon and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Duckworth said they "must reject this foolhardy plan and instead focus on increasing the safety of the airspace".The arch is to be built just outside Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, and about 4mi (6km) from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, the site of the deadly 2025 midair crash between a military helicopter and commercial plane.  "The American people cannot afford to stand witness to Trump's risky plan to place a 250-foot (72m) structure along a busy approach path, especially if he follows through on plans to station snipers on the arch and fly drones," Duckworth wrote in the letter, which was obtained by the BBC's US partner, CBS News. The FAA, however, ruled last week that the massive structure would not pose a risk to flights coming into and out of the airport. On Thursday, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, led by Trump appointees, announced it was ending required consultations with local officials about how the structure might affect 42 historic properties in the area.The council said in the announcement that the National Park Service, which oversees federal landmarks, had proposed a plan for mitigating potential harms to those properties, but local historic preservation officers "raised concerns with the purpose and need of the Triumphal Arch". They also questioned whether the service had adequately identified possible harms and planned sufficient actions to address them.Federal and state officials are not required to reach an agreement on a project's harm-mitigation plans, and those consultations are allowed to be terminated if both sides can't agree. The council expects to submit a final report on the process early next month.Meanwhile, Democratic Virginia Congressman Don Beyer says excavation work on the site where the arch will stand has already begun.Beyer, who is leading congressional opposition to the arch, said he found workers operating heavy equipment when he visited the site on Thursday who told him they were "conducting archaeological work to evaluate the composition of the soil". That is "deeply troubling", Beyer said, particularly because the administration is required to give 48 hours notice before work can begin. "The Administration appears to be pushing ahead with activity at the site even while it still has not done the basic work necessary to understand the consequences of this project," Beyer wrote.A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.

schema.headline: Trump's plans for massive arch move ahead

title: TikTok to pay $100m, limit daily child usage in Alabama settlement
description: TikTok and its parent company ByteDance will pay the US state of Alabama $100m (£754.5m) and make a series of changes to restrict children's usage in
body: TikTok and its parent company ByteDance will pay the US state of Alabama $100m (£754.5m) and make a series of changes to restrict children's usage in the state as part of a lawsuit settlement. The deal was reached just before a jury trial was set to begin on Monday. It ends a lawsuit alleging TikTok is intentionally designed to addict children to its features, mirroring a host of lawsuits against social media platforms. The company is now required to install a number of new safety features, including a two-hour daily usage limit for children as well as overnight and school-hour restrictions.The changes will only apply in Alabama. It marks the platform's first settlement with a US state. "We're very pleased," said Katherine Robertson, chief counsel in the Alabama Attorney General's office in an interview with the BBC.She added that the state had been engaged in mediation with TikTok in the run-up to trial and that the deal they have now reached was the state's final offer. "This is very restrictive injunctive relief that's going to require them to change a lot of the policies that we had identified as the culprits in what we call the war on childhood," Robertson said.The new time limits and usage blocks are due to take effect immediately. However, TikTok has up to a year to implement other changes included as part of the settlement, such as the establishment of age verification measures. Many of the measures follow a framework established by an August settlement struck between social media rival Meta and 52 state Attorneys General.TikTok has agreed to pay up to $300m to Alabama if conditions of the new settlement are not met. The $100m payment is due to the state within 45 days. Other safety features demanded as part of the deal include a host of measures to allow parents to heavily moderate usage by their children, along with restrictions on some content, and new ways to verify the age of young users. TikTok will also limit children's accounts being discovered by adults, and notify parents to any "suspicious interactions" between teen users and adult users. A blanket ban on all cosmetic filters for children will also be put in place. "TikTok's priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community," a spokesperson for TikTok USDS said. "This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens."Earlier this year, TikTok split its business ownership, with a new group of investors taking control of operations in the US. The remainder of the business is operated out of China.ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok in China, was also part of Friday's settlement as ByteDance remains a minority owner of the US joint venture.

schema.headline: TikTok to pay $100m, limit daily child usage in Alabama settlement

title: Russia-Ukraine war: Moscow targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on data centres, Zelensky says
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia has widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum dis
body: President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia has widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum disruption for ordinary people."All this affects people's ability to stay connected, study, work," he said.On Friday a Russian drone hit a business centre in the capital Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. A separate attack killed a 14-year-old boy. Israel's foreign ministry said he was an Israeli citizen.Russia confirmed it had targeted a data centre site, saying it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence.About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages on Wednesday due to strikes.Some firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.In the north-western city of Lutsk, electronic information boards at public transport stops were not working on Friday, officials said. The city council said this was "due to damage caused by a Russian attack on data centres in Kyiv".In Friday's social media post, Zelensky wrote: "The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centres, internet providers – for Russia, all ordinary life is simply a target."It is important that the world responds to all of this and that Russia feels the response to its terror."Late on Friday, Zelensky said "additional decisions" had been made at his meeting with Ukraine's top defence and security officials to protect the country's data centres and other critical communications facilities to ensure their continuous operation. Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has said that Russia was seeking to disrupt the flow of "life-saving information" by targeting data centres."Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives. This is critical civilian infrastructure... It is not a military target. It is essential to keeping everyday life functioning," Sybiha said.Zelensky's top adviser on defence technologies on Thursday admitted that "there may be local disruptions" following Russian attacks an the cost of internet services could increase to cover the costs of repairs.But Serhii Beskrestnov stressed that Ukraine's internet network was highly decentralised, so the country "will not be left without internet access". The data centre hit by Russia on Friday was run by Datagroup. The company said its specialists were assessing the damage after the daytime attack but all services "continue to operate from backup sites".Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said on Friday evening that seven people had been killed and 59 injured after Russian overnight attacks.Russia's defence ministry later confirmed it had hit the Datagroup site, which it said was being used by the Ukrainian military's intelligence.Footage showing the damaged Inkom business centre that housed Datagroup has since been verified by the BBC.The Russian defence ministry also said that over the past few days its forces have targeted a number of data processing and telecommunications centres in Ukraine, including New-Telco, United DC, Kyivstar and Parkovyi.In recent weeks, Moscow has also intensified its strikes on Ukraine's energy and railway infrastructure – seeking to cause maximum damage as winter approaches.Ukraine's military has been hitting Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, saying they help finance Russia's ongoing war effort.Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.Speaking to reporters late on Friday, Putin said Moscow would "give careful thought" to the idea of resuming direct peace negotiations with Kyiv, citing last week's "massive" Ukrainian attack on the capital Moscow and other recent strikes."It's all possible," he said, but stressed that Ukraine "must feel our retaliatory strikes",  and that all decisions would be taken "based on the Russian Federation's interests".Zelensky had earlier said he was ready for trilateral talks that would also involve the US.Kyiv and its European allies have repeatedly accused Putin of rejecting any peace negotiations, saying he was seeking to seize more Ukrainian territory.Speaking to the media, Putin also restated his position that Moscow had "no plans" and "no reason" to attack Europe. He had made similar statements about Ukraine, before launching his full-scale invasion almost five years ago.In a separate development on Friday, the European Union agreed to release €6.6bn for Ukraine, the bloc's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said, describing this as "good news for Ukraine and bad news for Russia".This includes €900 million for the EU's Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine, and a €1 billion fund for joint procurement of equipment, she said on X. "Moscow's hybrid attacks try to intimidate Europe into scaling back its support for Ukraine. Europe is doing the opposite."Meanwhile, Poland's prosecutors opened an investigation in what they said was an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station in Wola Krobowska on Wednesday.In a statement, the national prosecutor's office said "there is a reasonable suspicion... that the perpetrators acted on the orders of the Russian special services". Moscow has not commented.The station transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have warned Russia may be preparing hybrid attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

schema.headline: Russia-Ukraine war: Moscow targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on data centres, Zelensky says

title: Super League play-off semi-final: Leeds Rhinos 12-14 Warrington Wolves - Wolves reach Grand Final
description: Betfred Super League play-off semi-finalLeeds (12) 12Tries: Hall, Connor Goals: Connor 2Warrington (12) 14Tries: Bentley, Yates Goals: Irwin 3Warringt
body: Betfred Super League play-off semi-finalLeeds (12) 12Tries: Hall, Connor Goals: Connor 2Warrington (12) 14Tries: Bentley, Yates Goals: Irwin 3Warrington Wolves have reached their first Super League Grand Final in eight years with a thrilling victory against Leeds Rhinos at AMT Headingley Stadium.In a tense and topsy-turvy semi-final the sides traded two first-half tries each and were locked at 12-12 at the break, before the Wolves were awarded a contentious penalty which was slotted nervelessly by 18-year-old Ewan Irwin to nudge them ahead.Half-back Jake Connor scored 10 points for an injury-depleted Rhinos, including a first-half try which he inventively created in midfield, and attempted a goal-kick from 62 metres out with the final play of the game but the ball landed short of the sticks.The Wolves will face the winners of either Wigan Warriors or Wakefield Trinity in the showpiece final at Old Trafford next Saturday, as they stand just one win away from a first league title since 1955.Leeds limped into the semi-final missing a number of key players including the league's top try-scorer Maika Sivo, captain Ash Handley, and Man of Steel nominee Lachie Miller.The Rhinos were dealt with a further injury blow moments before kick-off when Chris Hankinson pulled up in the warm-up and had to be replaced by Ned McCormack in the starting line-up.Warrington breached Leeds' inexperienced backline after five minutes as England captain George Williams' pinpoint kick was met by Matty Ashton, who helped find former Rhino James Bentley to slide over for an early score.Brodie Croft's cut-out pass found Ryan Hall to score his 358th career try to draw level with former Wakefield legend Neil Fox in the all-time scorers list, as Connor nailed the extras from touch to drag Leeds level.Connor was then involved at the other end of the field, teaming up with young full-back Fergie McCormack to usher Albert Hopoate into touch as he threatened to score and moments later Arron Lindop collided with team-mate Hopoate as the Wolves again squandered a certain four points.Leeds made the Wolves pay soon later as they raced down field. A delicate kick over the top from Connor bounced kindly for McCormack, and once Kallum Watkins found Connor he was not to be denied by Ashton's scrambling defending, using his momentum to spin and crash down.Leeds Rhinos head coach Brad Arthur said:"I've not whinged or complained the whole time I've been here. I'm extremely proud of our team and our club and players."I don't know what more we could have really done. We got a couple of bits and pieces wrong but so did they. It just would have been really nice if the game was decided by an individual or a piece of skill."We're talking about a field goal or something like that rather than a soft penalty to decide such a big game. It is a soft penalty."Ned got escorted four or five times tonight on kicks and I wasn't expecting penalties for them. But that's a soft penalty to decide such a big game."Warrington Wolves captain George Williams told BBC Radio Merseyside:"Nerve-wracking, mad game, just pleased we've came through the other side. "Credit to Leeds, they gave it a good crack. They've been a great team all year but we rode the waves and the main thing is we're through to the big dance next week."They were probably dominant for the first 20 [minutes], we came home strong in the back end [of the first half]. It's no good for the nerves but sometimes it's better when you're out there, you can do something about it."[On earning the match-winning penalty] "People think it might be a bit controversial but I was chasing the ball and I got a little nudge. I was off balance and nowadays, with the escorts, they give them. Luckily, it went to us and that was the game."Leeds: F. McCormack; Lumb, N. McCormack, Newman, Hall; Croft, Connor; Oledzki, O'Connor, Lodge, Watkins, McDonnell, Palasia.Interchanges: Holroyd, Jenkins, Smith, Cassell.Warrington: Josh Thewlis; Hopoate, Lindop, King, Ashton; Williams, Irwin; Byrne, Walker, Harrison, Bentley, Stone, Currie.Interchanges: Yates, Powell, Philbin, Tanginoa.Referee: Chris Kendall.

schema.headline: Super League play-off semi-final: Leeds Rhinos 12-14 Warrington Wolves - Wolves reach Grand Final

title: Could an iced coffee freeze you out of the job market?
description: Figure caption, Watch: Is it OK to take an iced coffee to a job interview?ByJemma Crew and Daniel ThomasBusiness reportersWould you bring an iced coff
body: Figure caption, Watch: Is it OK to take an iced coffee to a job interview?ByJemma Crew and Daniel ThomasBusiness reportersWould you bring an iced coffee to a job interview?The question on the internet's lips this week started life, as many do, in a TikTok video. "Don't waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee, it just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand," said US recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen.It's what her Gen Z job candidates are doing, she said, warning it makes it look like the interview is "just a stop on your list of errands for the day".The post has started what Wehniainen calls the Great Iced Coffee Debate of 2026.Some believe turning up with an iced matcha latte in hand is a cardinal sin. They say it's unprofessional, too informal, and a distraction.Others feel this is an overreaction - distracting from how difficult it is to secure a job - or even just get an interview in the first place.In a subsequent LinkedIn post, Wehniainen says she "was never saying that bringing coffee makes someone a bad candidate. "My point was simply about avoiding distractions."Hanad, 28, works for an energy supplier in London. He likes iced coffee but wouldn't bring one to an interview."A job interview is all about first impressions," he says. "Anything can deter the employer from employing you."Iced coffee is something a lot of teens drink… it would look immature and too informal."Image caption, Hanad says he wouldn't take an iced coffee to an interviewHe would never bring along an energy drink for the same reasons. But he says water or a hot coffee would be okay.His colleague Tsvetina, 24, thinks a potential employee shouldn't be judged by what they bring to the interview, nor their dress code."I think we should be moving away from these traditional corporate stigmas. What matters is what the person is actually communicating during the interview."Aisha, 28, says she would take along an iced coffee. "I think it shows that I have come early enough to get iced coffee."She wouldn't bring a fizzy drink, however.In general, she thinks a lot of employers like to see personality in a candidate. "It makes you stand out from other people who are coming [applying] for the job."Image caption, Katy feels there is a sexist element to the controversary around Wehniainen's postKaty, 25, a personal assistant in events, says she personally wouldn't turn up to a job interview with an iced coffee.But she sees the controversy around Wehniainen's post as "a bit sexist, because it's usually girls who drink iced coffee"."If it was a hot coffee, which is more masculine, there wouldn't be a discourse about that."Young people trying to land their first job are facing multiple challenges.The number of graduate vacancies in the UK has almost halved in the past year, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.Around one in eight people aged 16-24 are not in education, employment or training - so called Neets.Young workers in the US are also struggling with a tight jobs market, external as hiring slows.'A little bit flippant'Lucy Cooper is the founder of Spark, a design and branding recruitment company in London.She says her industry - marketing - is really tough right now, and she doesn't know of any Gen Z candidates who would risk turning up to an interview with an iced coffee.You could "seem too relaxed and a little bit flippant, like you're not taking it seriously enough, or you are interviewing the employer rather than the other way round"."I think people at junior level are very conscious about not doing anything that could jeopardise their chances," she says.She adds that it would be fine to accept a coffee offered by the employer, however, or drink one on a video interview. Dan Craddock, director at Hays, says employers shouldn't rely on "snap judgements"."It's important not to read too much into a single item a candidate brings to an interview. "Whether that's an iced coffee, a bottle of water or a notebook, employers are ultimately assessing the skills, experience and behaviours that will make someone successful in the role."Chris Mason, co-founder of Intelligent People - a specialist recruitment agency for the tech industry, says focusing on ice coffees alone "does seem to be an overreaction on the US recruiter's part".He advises candidates to "try to do everything possible to project the right image and attitude".He warns bringing snacks or specialist drinks may undermine the impression candidates will want to give - that they're "serious and focused on the interview".He says the main issue they see with some younger candidates is a lack of preparation, not being punctual, and not researching the role, organisation or interviewer.

schema.headline: Could an iced coffee freeze you out of the job market?

title: British climber dies after falling 60m on Spanish mountainside
description: A 28-year-old British climber has died after falling about 60m (200ft) from one of the highest mountains in northern Spain. The man fell into a gully
body: A 28-year-old British climber has died after falling about 60m (200ft) from one of the highest mountains in northern Spain. The man fell into a gully while descending from the summit of Torrecerredo in the Cantabrian Mountains on Thursday, the Spanish Civil Guard said.Police and an air unit were deployed to the scene after emergency services were called around 13:27 local time (11:27 GMT). The man's body was recovered by a mountain rescue unit. The UK Foreign Office said it was in contact with local authorities "following reports of the death of a British national in Spain".Spanish emergency services said they initially received a call saying that a person had fallen on the eastern face of the mountain and dispatched a rescue group aboard a medical helicopter.A doctor among them confirmed the man's death at about 14:18 and remained at the scene to guard the body until a Civil Guard helicopter could arrive about an hour and 20 minutes later.Specialist mountain rescuers were then lowered by winch to the site of the accident, where they recovered the man's body and belongings.The identity of the climber, who Spanish authorities said was English, has not been given. The accident occurred when he was about 20 metres from the mountain's summit.His body has been transported to the Institute of Legal Medicine, which provides forensic pathology services, in Asturias, the Civil Guard said.Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of about 2,650m, is in the Picos de Europa, which is popular with climbers and walkers.The region's tourism board describes the route up the mountain as "very difficult" with a demanding ascent, warning climbers to take particular care on steep and exposed upper sections on their way down.Sepa Asturias - the body responsible for emergency services in the region - said it also transported a 54-year-old French woman to hospital after she suffered a leg injury on the mountain range on Thursday afternoon.

schema.headline: British climber dies after falling 60m on Spanish mountainside

title: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged'
description: Warning: This story contains distressing detailsPolice in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead befor
body: Warning: This story contains distressing detailsPolice in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" and placed hanging in a tree.The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs.The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests. In a news release, police said that the medical examiner had determined that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging was staged.Fortune's mother told the BBC that she remembers the coroner telling her: "we're not treating this as [an] actual hanging." Her daughter, they told her, was dead before being placed in the tree. Spivey also recalled police telling her the incident was "drug related".Speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday, Spivey described how she knows her daughter fought for her life till the very end."I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey told reporters. Fortune leaves behind four young children, ages 7, 5, 4 and 1, she added.Dressed in a shirt that reads "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she does not want to see any innocent people going to jail."I just hope they have the right people," she said.Three people have so far been arrested in relation to the case, all of whom are black, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody in without bond.A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in the case this week.A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday.The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country. Representative Ayanna Pressley, Democrat of Massachusetts, cites at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress, external, which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers. The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has been ruled a suicide.

schema.headline: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged'

title: U2 celebrate 50th anniversary at the school where they formed
description: Figure caption, Watch: U2 return to school where everything started for their 50th anniversaryByMusic correspondentExactly 50 years after they formed,
body: Figure caption, Watch: U2 return to school where everything started for their 50th anniversaryByMusic correspondentExactly 50 years after they formed, U2 returned to Dublin to play a gig at the school where they met."We've escaped from the lab," declared Bono, as the quartet took to a stage in the playground. "How's the experiment working for you?"The pupils of Mount Temple Comprehensive may not have been born when U2 were the world’s biggest band, but they gave them a hero's welcome, waving signs that said, "I love U2", "It's a beautiful day - no school", and, "Bono, my mum says hi!" The group treated them to a career-spanning set that included hits like I Will Follow, Vertigo and With Or Without You, as well as their latest single, Silencio. As they played, teachers pulled down pupils who’d climbed on their classmates' shoulders, before getting swept up in the moment and dancing along themselves.As he looked out from the same stage where U2 made their debut in 1976, Bono became emotional. "Thanks for, er… Yeah... I didn't… Wow," said the frontman, temporarily lost for words. Image caption, U2 were all pupils at Mount Temple Comprehensive School in the mid-1970sImage source, U2Image caption, The band played their first gig at a school talent competition, covering Peter Frampton's Show Me The Way and Bye Bye Baby by the Bay City RollersImage source, Rich FuryImage caption, The band played seven songs at the end of the school day: I Will Follow, Vertigo, Beautiful Day, Out of Control, Silencio, One and With or Without YouImage source, Rich FuryImage caption, Pupils clamoured to meet the band, who have sold more than 175 million records worldwideThe U2 story began in those same halls and corridors five decades ago, when 14-year-old Larry Mullen Jr pinned a handwritten note to the school noticeboard."Drummer seeks musicians to form band." Auditions were held a couple of days later, on 25 September, 1976, in Larry's parents' kitchen. Among the hopeful "misfits", as their school-friend Frank Kearns called them, were Bono, The Edge and Adam Clayton – who arrived wearing a full-length Afghan coat.Initially called Feedback, and then The Hype, they conquered the world as U2, transforming themselves from a scrappy punk outfit into stadium-conquering rock titans, whose big ideas and big anthems attracted millions of admirers, and almost as many detractors.Speaking to BBC News, Mullen confessed the infamous wanted advert had been his father's idea all along."I'd been playing on my own, in my house, and my dad was pretty frustrated," he says."I wasn't very good at many things, and playing the drums was included in that. So I think he, out of frustration, said I should try and play with other people.""And unfortunately," adds Bono, "he got the three of us."Image source, James MahonImage caption, The group honed their skills over dozens of gigs in the Dublin venue McGonaglesBono, then known as Paul Hewson, had actually been tempted to skip the audition. He was two years older, and concerned about looking out of place."I wouldn't be hanging out with second years, and particularly really good-looking ones," he says.Eventually, his friend Reggie Manuel persuaded him to attend, even giving him a lift on his rickety old motorbike."I can tell myself it was a Harley Davidson," the singer jokes, "but really it was a Yamaha DX100."The first band practice didn't exactly show promise. There was more talking than playing. Clayton, a bassist who couldn't play bass, was selected on account of having "the best hair". And Bono, who wanted to be the guitarist, didn't bring a guitar."I was never any good with gear," he reflects. "Carrying it, unpacking it, that kind of thing."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The quartet have remained friends since 1976, partly due to a decision to split all their earnings equallyEven so, there were signs the band would attract an adoring legion of fans. Half-way through the rehearsal, a group of screaming girls tried to climb the garden wall.For Clayton, that was the moment that sealed the deal."Larry already had a fan club, and we thought, 'Well, if he's got a fan club, that looks pretty good to us. Maybe if we hang out with this guy, it might stretch a little further'."Mullen, forever the band's stoic moral compass, was not impressed by the invasion."As I recall, Larry Mullen took a hose to the fans," laughs Bono."I don't know what possessed me," the drummer grimaces, while trying to insist the hosing  "was an act of kindness and love because it was a hot day"."They enjoyed it," he protests. "It was playful."Bono jumps in to save his friend's embarrassment…. Well, kind of."It's been the story of our lives ever since. He doesn't even want to have fans, but we quite like them."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The 1992 Zoo TV Tour pushed the boundaries of what was possible in a stadium show, ushering in an era of video screens and multimedia backdropsFrom that kitchen in Rosemount Avenue, U2 became the world's biggest rock band.Anthems like With Or Without You, One and Beautiful Day have always sounded majestic yet personal; powered by The Edge's cascading guitar tone and Bono's lyrics which, for all their proselytising, remain grounded in a belief in humanity.They made a stylistic swerve in the 1990s, embracing electronics, dance music and irony on the albums Achtung Baby, Zooropa and Pop.Along the way, they reinvented stadium concerts with the Zoo TV tour, whose stage was crammed full of multimedia screens and satellite feeds, while Bono made nightly prank calls to the White House.The Edge, real name Dave Evans, puts their longevity down to a lack of formal training."It's been a guiding light, in some ways, the limitations of the band," he explains."We're in this place where, musically, we never know what's about to happen. It can fall apart or it can become something extraordinary."And that's the beauty of U2.”Back on stage at Mount Temple, Bono paid tribute to his alma matter for allowing the band to flourish. The support of teachers allowed them to realise that “maybe all we needed was around us, just under our feet,” he said. And he dedicated the performance to school councillor Jack Heaslip, who later became a “travelling pastor” on the band’s tours, before his death from motor neurone disease in 2015. U2 then closed their set with an orchestral arrangement of One, assisted by students from Ireland's Music Generation education programme, which they helped fund and establish 15 years ago. New music includes Dolly Parton duetA few hours earlier, the band announced their 16th studio album, Carnaval de Luz, which will be released in November.It's a companion piece to February's angry, impassioned EP, Days of Ash, which tackled headlines about ICE killings in America, the war in Ukraine and the Israel-Palestine conflict.That was followed by the more sedate Easter Lily EP in April; with Carnaval de Luz rounding off the story.The Edge described it as "a messy, provocative, sacred collection of songs", while Bono promised "loud guitars, deep bass [and] ecstatic rhythms."Closing out the album's 12 tracks is Torn, a song co-written by Dolly Parton, which was the country icon's final recorded performance before her death last month.In a press release, the track was described as "a tender country song detailing broken family ties, that holds wider resonances".BBC News will run an interview about that song, and the rest of the album, in the coming weeks.

schema.headline: U2 celebrate 50th anniversary at the school where they formed

title: E-bikes seized by police sold on at auction, BBC finds
description: E-bikes seized by police forces in the UK are being sold on at auction, despite some fears they could end up back in the hands of criminals, the BBC c
body: E-bikes seized by police forces in the UK are being sold on at auction, despite some fears they could end up back in the hands of criminals, the BBC can reveal.Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally, or used in a crime - most are later destroyed, but a BBC investigation has found some are sold on to members of the public in online auctions.Across the UK, police sold 161 e-bikes last year and 54 in 2024, although the real number could be higher because not every force responded to the BBC's Freedom of Information request.Some of the forces said they had now ended the practice, but others defended it as a way of putting "money back into policing".Six forces responded to say e-bikes they had seized had been sold, including large forces such as West Midlands Police and Police Scotland.The figure includes electrically-assisted pedal cycles, which look similar to bicycles and have a motor that kicks in as a rider pedals, as well as electric motorbikes, which are usually more powerful and are propelled only by their motor.E-bikes have become controversial because some think they are linked to crime and anti-social behaviour.Recent BBC reporting has highlighted cases across the country of balaclava-clad young men riding illegally on footpaths and intimidating residents.  There have also been a number of pedestrian deaths, including 86-year-old grandmother Gloria Stephenson, who was struck at a zebra crossing in Sunderland last year by an illegal e-motorbike.Police Scotland, which covers the whole country, says it sends seized e-bikes to an accredited recycler who may then decide to auction them, with money going back to the force. Last year 93 e-bikes seized by Police Scotland were sold, more than any other force. Two e-bikes seized by West Yorkshire Police last year were sold at auction. The force said any money raised from the auctions was split between the force and the West Yorkshire Combined Authority, and said some cash went to "local good causes". All of those sold were "legally compliant", they added.West Midlands Police, which sold 12 e-bikes last year, said the "vast majority" of seized bikes were destroyed, with a "small number" sold "via an independent auction company so that the money can be put back into policing".The BBC found some forces had also sold e-scooters. It is illegal to use a privately-owned e-scooter on public property, although owning an e-scooter is not illegal.Durham Constabulary sold three of them last year, and West Mercia Police sold one. West Mercia's force also sold 24 e-bikes.Both forces told the BBC they have recently reviewed their policy and they will no longer sell e-bikes or e-scooters.Clive Grunshaw, the Police and Crime Commissioner for Lancashire said: "There's nowhere apart from [a] back garden that these scooters can be legally used, so it's a confused message," he said.He urged police forces to stop selling e-bikes, which he said have become the "transport of choice for drug gangs" because they are "so difficult to catch".He suspects that some criminals whose vehicles are seized simply try to buy them back from auction websites.Grunshaw worries some criminals are buying legally compliant e-bikes from police and then giving them illegal modifications.Legal electric pedal bikes are restricted so they cannot drive faster than 15.5mph, but criminals can buy "tuning kits" online, often from eastern Europe, allowing some to travel faster than 40mph.Durham Constabulary, which sold 29 e-bikes last year, told the BBC they had recently reviewed its policy, and they "will now be crushed without exception".Greater Manchester Police sold one e-bike last year.Police tend to sell the vehicles through commercial auction websites like Raw2k, a company listed by several forces.The website regularly advertises e-bikes as "sold at the direction of police", including a Chinese-manufactured electric dirt bike that it says was auctioned from Falkirk earlier this month, with an opening price of £250 (much less than the £3,295 listed as the retail price for a new model).

schema.headline: E-bikes seized by police sold on at auction, BBC finds

title: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
description: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.Arag
body: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June."The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar.Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues. Earlier this week, US President Donald Trump threatened to "annihilate the Islamic Republic".The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November."If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi told reporters.He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU". "I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he added.A US official told the BBC that the US was "in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush".The MOU between the US and Iran, signed on 18 June, was designed to bring about a ceasefire and at least partly reopen the Strait of Hormuz. The 14-point agreement said Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. It noted that the US, Iran and their allies would end military operations on "all fronts" and contained provisions including the end of a US naval blockade and sanctions relief. It also said Iran would "make arrangements using its best efforts for the safe passage of commercial vessels" through the strait and hold talks with Oman over future shipping arrangements.But it fell apart a short time later when both sides resumed strikes.Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation.The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. It has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing huge disruption to the Iranian economy.Trump since has claimed the US has been successful in getting oil out through the Strait of Hormuz. Shipping data shows a recent 10-day average of about 18 transits per day, with daily numbers dropping as low as nine vessels on certain days, according to Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm cited by Reuters.However, Yemen's Houthis - allied to Iran - have recently intensified attacks aimed at disrupting oil exports from Saudi Arabia via the Red Sea on the other side of the Arabian peninsula.The group seized large strategically important stretches of the Red Sea coast in a rapid offensive this month, including the port of Mokha, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait, another chokepoint for global shipping.

schema.headline: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
